Space had just opened to mankind when the General Assembly set its first rules of law in Resolution 1962, adopted on 13 December 1963. The text is a declaration of legal principles for the work of states in space. It hails the vast prospects that man's entry into space has opened, and the shared stake of all mankind in its peaceful study and use.

Space work, the principles hold, must serve the good of all states, rich or poor in science and wealth. Joint work in space, both in science and in law, will build trust and warm ties between peoples. These nine principles became the seed of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, still the base law of space.

Ukraine's unity and land, within its known borders, are backed in full. Michael Schillaci asked in 2006 whether the contest for mates helped grow the primate brain. Brain size varies widely among primates, from tiny monkeys to apes and humans. Natural selection for survival skills is the usual explanation. Sexual selection, the pressure of competing for mates, is the rival Schillaci tested.

Comparing brain size across primate species against the strength of mating competition in each, he weighed whether the two rise together. A link would mean the social and sexual arena, not just food and tools, drove brain evolution. That possibility matters for the biggest version of the question: how humans ended up with brains so costly and so large.

Minutes of the Joint Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 record an evening session at half past nine. Ambassador Harriman briefed the chiefs on the Soviet attitude ahead of the Tehran meeting. General Marshall had asked him to speak to the proposals of the Joint Strategic Survey Committee.

Harriman expects no detailed Soviet strategy plan, since Moscow is wholly absorbed in its own fighting, and he warns against arriving with a cut-and-dried plan of their own. The Soviets hate being handed finished decisions, he says, but frank explanation has worked well, and Stalin has already told his people a second front is coming soon. Harriman also reports strong Soviet pressure to end the war fast, and a firm intent to join the war on Japan once Germany falls.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d362:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the dinner conversation at Tehran on 28 November 1943, beginning at half past eight in the evening. After talk of where the leaders might meet next, with Fairbanks in Alaska favored, Stalin opens the question of France's future.

Stalin argues at length that France's ruling class is rotten to the core. It delivered the country to Germany. It deserves neither gentle treatment nor her empire back, since no strategic points can safely be left in French hands. Roosevelt partly agrees, naming New Caledonia and Dakar as points needing trusteeship or firm control. Churchill answers that the four victorious nations must hold the world's strategic points. On Germany, Roosevelt wants the very word Reich struck out; Stalin replies that the Reich itself must be made impotent, and presses for stronger measures than either Western leader names.

frus-1944-quebec-d162:

London's preferred option, a British fleet under American command in the main operations, was not the one Washington accepted here.

Instead the Americans accepted the alternative: a British Empire task force under a British commander, built from British, Australian, and New Zealand land, sea, and air forces. It would operate in the Southwest Pacific under General MacArthur's supreme command. The chiefs noted this would still place the British Fleet well to reinforce the American Pacific Fleet if later desired.

The restatement replaced the older formula in C.C.S. 417/2. It was accepted subject to the assurances the British had requested and the Americans had given in the preceding papers of the series.

The objective was to force Japan's unconditional surrender in two ways. First, lower her ability and will to resist by sea and air blockade, intensive bombardment, and destruction of her air and naval strength. Second, invade and seize objectives in her industrial heart. Marshall had explained the new wording was designed to allow for invasion of the home islands.

Churchill proposes barring the press from the conference, code-named Argonaut, entirely. Each leader could still bring three or four uniformed service photographers. Their still and motion pictures would be released only when the leaders chose. He also expects the usual agreed communiqué at the end. Max Muller delivered four lectures at the Royal Institution in London to introduce a new field: the science of religion. Published in book form in 1882, the lectures argue that faiths can be studied side by side, with the same calm methods used on language or nature. Contempt and blind belief both bar the way.

Muller sorts religions, traces their growth, and pleads for fairness toward creeds not one's own. His own field, the tongues of India, supplies much of the evidence. Verified from the 1919 edition, the lectures state the great orientalist's method plainly. Comparative religion as a discipline starts, in public, here.
tob-14462:
The Mahatma Letters are letters said to come from hidden masters, Koot Hoomi and Morya, to A. P. Sinnett and A. O. Hume in the 1880s. They arrived by odd means in India, through Helena Blavatsky's circle. No set of papers in theosophy has stirred more debate.

The letters teach theosophical cosmology: rounds of worlds, root races, karma, and the hidden brotherhood guiding mankind. They also give sharp personal advice and scolding to the two Englishmen. Believers treat them as scripture of the movement; critics call them fakes. Either way, they shaped the Theosophical Society from its early years.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Between 1954 and 1962 the United States built a nuclear presence across Western Europe, stationing American weapons with allied forces under shared-control arrangements. This briefing-book page is the first part of an Archive set on that deployment. The evidence here is the title alone, and the documents in this part are not described. Those years set the pattern that still governs American weapons in Europe: bombs stored on allied soil, owned by Washington, and surrounded by political arrangements every host government must defend.
wilson-prehistoric-man-1862:
Daniel Wilson, a Scottish scholar who became a Toronto professor, published Prehistoric Man in 1862. Wilson had coined the word 'prehistoric' in English a decade earlier. His book researches the origin of civilization in both the Old World and the New, the first systematic account of North American archaeology beside the European evidence.

He treats the mounds, earthworks, and copper tools of North America as seriously as Europe's barrows and flints. Against the fashion of his day, he argues the continent's ancient works were built by ancestors of its native peoples. The book is generous, learned, and early. It helped found archaeology in Canada and the United States.
huxley-on-fossil-remains-of-man-1862:
Thomas Henry Huxley, Darwin's most forceful defender, lectured on fossil human remains in 1862. He spoke at the Royal Institution with very little material to work from. The Engis and Neanderthal skulls formed nearly the whole evidence.

Huxley compares those skulls with modern human and ape skulls, bone by bone. He finds no barrier that separates fossil humans from living ones. The lecture builds a Darwinian reading of human antiquity from scant bones. Its confidence helped set the tone for his famous book on man's place in nature the next year.
randolph-dealings-with-the-dead-1862:
Paschal Beverly Randolph launched his strange career with Dealings with the Dead, his book of 1862. Randolph was a Black sage, healer, and seer in the United States. He claimed gifts of sight and a rank in the Rosy Cross. Here he tells of talks with the dead and what they taught him.

Grief, hope, and the fate of the soul fill the pages. His voice is bold, warm, and sure of its path. The book is the first stone of the Rosy Cross in his land. It shows a rare, brave mind at work. Randolph sailed, wed, and built bands in a life of bold turns. He wrote as he lived: fast, warm, and sure of his strange path.
turgenev-fathers-and-sons-1862:
Ivan Turgenev published Fathers and Sons in 1862, the novel that named an age's philosophy in one word, nihilism. The nihilist Bazarov clashes with the older generation in a book that angered young and old alike on publication. Turgenev claimed to love Bazarov most, though critics of both camps accused him of betrayal.

Arkady brings his friend Bazarov, a medical student, home to his father Nikolai and uncle Pavel. Bazarov scorns art, authority, and romance, dissects frogs, and duels Pavel over a morning's insult at Marino. He loves the cool widow Odintsova, is refused, and dies of typhus caught at a peasant's autopsy, asking her blessing at home. His parents' grief at the village grave closes a book far tenderer than its famous label suggests to most readers. The novel remains the classic account of a generation gap.
spencer-first-principles-1862:
Herbert Spencer published First Principles in 1862, the opening volume of his System of Synthetic Philosophy. Spencer argues that evolution is a universal law for all things. Matter integrates and motion dissipates, from nebulae to societies and minds. His phrase survival of the fittest, coined here, became famous worldwide.

The first part treats the unknowable, the realm beyond science and religion alike. The second part states the laws of the knowable in abstract form. Spencer aimed to unify all science under one principle. Later science outgrew much of the system. The book remains a bold monument of Victorian system-building.
mommsen-history-rome-vol-1-1862:
Theodor Mommsen's History of Rome appears here in William P. Dickson's translation of 1862. Volume 1 covers Rome from its legendary founding to the eve of the Punic Wars. Mommsen rebuilds the early Republic: its laws, tribes, wars, and constitution. His learning drew on inscriptions and coins as well as texts.

Mommsen writes with the confidence of a liberal who knew modern politics too. His Rome feels alive, partisan, and legally precise. The work later won him the Nobel Prize in Literature. No reconstruction of the Republic has replaced his in scope. Volume 1 is the gateway to a monumental history. Dickson's version served English readers for generations.
van-helmont-oriatrike-1662:
Jean Baptiste van Helmont was a Flemish physician whose Ortus Medicinae reshaped seventeenth-century medicine. Chandler's 1662 English translation, Oriatrike, or Physick Refined, carried his Paracelsian chemical medicine to English readers. Van Helmont trusted the furnace and the balance as much as the ancient authors.

He teaches that life runs by ferments and by the archeus, an inner governor seated in the stomach's region. Fevers, stones, and plagues get new explanations in chemical terms, with cures drawn from mineral and plant preparations. His system broke Galen's long rule and taught doctors to think of the body as a chemical workshop.
gadbury-collectio-geniturarum-1662:
John Gadbury was a Restoration astrologer who feuded in print with rivals for decades. His Collectio Geniturarum, published in 1662, gathers a collection of one hundred and fifty nativities, birth charts of real people. The book is the great Restoration case-book of judicial astrology.

Each chart comes with the events of the life it maps: offices, marriages, illnesses, and deaths read against the planets. Gadbury meant the cases to prove the art by its hits, as a lawyer proves a rule by precedents. Students of the period still mine his collection for the lives it records in passing.
plos-pone-0003462:
Xiu-Feng Wan and co-authors traced bird flu change in Vietnam for this 2008 paper. Highly pathogenic H5N1 viruses caused heavy losses in the poultry industry. By June 2008, Vietnam held nearly a third of confirmed human cases worldwide. The team compared virus samples gathered between 2001 and 2007.

Reading the family tree of those samples showed how the virus evolved. Lineages rose, spread, and replaced each other over the years. Such maps warn which virus lines may threaten birds and people next. The work supports flu watch programs across the region. Vietnam's mix of farms and wild birds makes such tracking hard but vital.
plos-pone-0003562:
Lisa J. Ma and co-authors studied cell transfer through breastfeeding in mice in this 2008 paper. Nursing shapes the young immune system well beyond simple antibody cover. Immune cells from milk can cross the pup's gut lining. The team examined what that transfer does once pups grow up.

Non-transgenic pups were fostered to test the transfer cleanly. As adults, recipients showed altered delayed-type hypersensitivity responses. The effect also differed by the recipient's gender. Milk thus passes living immune education from mother to young. Nursing effects like these may reach well into adult health and disease risk.
plos-pone-0003662:
Karen M. J. van Loo, Tim Dejaegere, Martine van Zweeden, and colleagues published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Atherosclerosis, the clogging of arteries, comes from genes and environment acting together. Based on rat work, the team suspected a role for the gamma-secretase complex.

They tested a variant in that complex for links to early coronary disease. The variant tracked with premature clogged heart arteries in men, but not in women. A male-only link like this adds a sex-specific piece to the puzzle of why heart disease strikes some people young.
plos-pone-0003762:
Walter S. Leal and Yuko Ishida published this fire ant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The red imported fire ant is an invasive pest with painful, sometimes dangerous stings. Its colonies come in two social forms, with one queen or many. Proteins called GP-9s were suspected of steering that social order by smell.

The authors found GP-9 proteins are in fact everywhere in the ant, not tied to smell organs. That makes them unlikely to run the social organization through scent. The negative result sends the search for the colony's chemical code in a new direction.
plos-pone-0003862:
Chao Tian, Roman Kosoy, Annette Lee, and colleagues published this population genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hidden ancestry differences within a study population can create false hits in disease gene hunts. As such hunts expand to new continental groups, their internal substructure must be mapped first. East Asia was the focus here.

Using genome-wide SNP arrays, the team charted genetic substructure across East Asian populations. The map shows how groups within the region relate and differ. Gene hunters can use it to avoid type 1 errors caused by ancestry rather than disease.
plos-pone-0003962:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Silke A. Schäfer, and co-authors studied a new diabetes risk gene region in 2008. The region, MTNR1B, had just been tied to type 2 diabetes. It was also reported to affect fasting blood sugar levels. The gene makes a receptor for the hormone melatonin.

Their PLOS ONE article used a well-studied group at raised diabetes risk. They tested whether variants in MTNR1B track with insulin cell function. Pancreatic beta cells make insulin, and their failure drives diabetes. A gene that tunes those cells links sleep hormones to blood sugar control. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004062:
Kim Zarse and Michael Ristow tested antidepressant claims in worms in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Certain serotonin-blocking antidepressants had been said to extend worm lifespan. Mianserin and methiothepin were reported to mimic calorie restriction in C. elegans. Longer life in worms often excites aging researchers.

Zarse and Ristow report the opposite for the adult worms they tested. The drugs increased body fat and shortened lifespan in their hands. Conflicting results demand care before calling a drug anti-aging. The study shows how conditions can flip a lifespan claim. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004162:
Pan-Young Jeong and colleagues published this worm study in PLOS ONE in 2009. When the tiny worm C. elegans senses a pheromone that signals crowding and poor food, it can enter dauer. Dauer is a tough state built for long survival. The molecular path into dauer had stayed unclear.

The team tracked the full time course of molecular change as worms enter dauer, watching genes and metabolism shift step by step. Their data lay out the metabolic basis of the switch, showing what a worm burns and stores in this state. The map helps explain how animals remodel themselves to outlast hard times.
plos-pone-0004262:
Takuya Tamura and colleagues published this neurogenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In several neurodegenerative disorders, glial cells, the brain's support cells, are suspected of harming neurons. Whether this non-cell-autonomous harm is general, and whether it differs by disease, had not been established.

Working in fruit flies, the team expressed mutant ataxin-1 and huntingtin, the proteins behind two inherited brain diseases, only in glia. They report that this alone induces both developmental and late-onset neuronal pathologies. Damage that starts in support cells reframes how these diseases might be treated. The fly work isolates glia as a source of harm.
plos-pone-0004362:
Camelia Kuhnen and Joan Chiao published this behavioural genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Individuals vary in their willingness to take financial risks. The authors show that variants of two genes are major factors in that variation. The genes regulate dopamine and serotonin neurotransmission. Both were previously linked to emotional behaviour, anxiety, and addiction.

The genes are tagged by the variants 5-HTTLPR and DRD4. Linking them to financial risk connects money choices to brain chemistry. The study is an early example of genoeconomics, the attempt to find DNA roots of economic choices.
plos-pone-0004462: In 2009, Daehler timed island weed takeovers in Hawai'i. Short delays before weed spread were clocked in island test plots. The weeds spread much faster than hoped. The neat finding sharpens weed forecasts greatly. The island plots were run with care.
plos-pone-0004562: In 2009, Joo, Karrasch, and Mühlbauer found tomato extract a mixed bag for guts. Tomato lycopene extract blocked LPS-induced NF-κB signaling but worsened colitis. The extract calmed one pathway, inflamed another. The finding nuances food-as-medicine claims. The model was murine.
plos-pone-0004662: In 2009, Borlak and Niehof linked a common transplant drug to diabetes via faulty liver switches. Two liver switches broke down under the drug. The key factors faltered quite badly. The neat study informs drug choices. The grim complication is frequent.

stowe-pearl-orrs-island-1862:
Stowe set The Pearl of Orr's Island on the coast of Maine, where she spent her summers. Copyright dates of 1862 and 1890 appear in this Riverside Press printing of 1896. The tale centers on young Mara Lincoln, raised among fishermen and sailors on the island.

Her quiet love story unfolds against storms, wrecks, and the steady rhythms of seafaring life. Stowe writes with deep fondness for New England's maritime people and their hard, plain ways. Reform takes a back seat here to place, character, and the sea that shapes both. Many readers judge it her most purely lovely novel.
stowe-agnes-of-sorrento-1862:
Agnes of Sorrento appeared in 1862 and stands here as volume seven of Stowe's Riverside writings. The setting is Italy in the 1400s, in the seaside town of Sorrento. Young Agnes grows up in a devout home while the fierce preacher Savonarola shakes the cities near her.

Love, faith, and harsh church power cross in her story as she is pulled toward a convent. A young cavalier pulls her heart the other way, toward life and marriage. Stowe wrote the novel while grieving a son lost in the Civil War, by the v1 account. Its thoughts on suffering and faith run deeper than most of her tales.
homestead-act-1862:
Congress passed the Homestead Act in 1862, and Lincoln signed it into law. Any settler who farmed public land for five years could own it. One hundred sixty acres came free to those who proved the claim.

Millions of claims followed as families poured onto the plains. The family farm became national policy in the act's plain terms. Towns, schools, and whole states rose from its quarter-section grants. Native peoples paid the price as their lands passed to settlers. The law that settled a continent still shapes the West's map and memory. Its grid of farms can still be seen from any plane window.
cia-0000009862:

A report naming three deaths at once suggests a shared event or a single source for several losses. Officials would split the report into three men's files after checking. Each name then carried the province as his place of death. The entry preserves the joint report as it arrived, before that splitting into separate griefs.

The subject line names Chalk, one of the code words attached to the operation that ran the Soviet colonel Oleg Penkovsky. Penkovsky was then beginning to pass military secrets to the West, the most valuable haul of the Cold War.

The slip records the letter's routing rather than its contents. It shows how the case's paper was logged, numbered, and sent on under strict control. Small as it is, the form is one procedural trace of the great spy case's filing system.
cia-0000012762:
How would the communists react if the United States took certain steps in South Vietnam? Special estimate SNIE 10-4-61, from October 1961, games out the answers. Washington was then deepening its commitment to Saigon, and each new step risked a wider war with Hanoi, Beijing, or Moscow. The estimate lays the possible reactions out in order, from protest to escalation.

Gaming the other side's responses was the Cold War's highest staff art. The community's coordinated judgment carried weight at the summit. For readers, the paper shows the war's widening being rehearsed on paper before it was lived.

North Vietnamese and Viet Cong wounded, plus U.S. prisoners, were taken from South Vietnam to the north. The trip was long and hard for men who were hurt or bound. The note shows the road system that fed the northern camps.

cia-0000037162:

Inside, the allegation is set down so it can be checked against other records. Late claims of this kind were hard to prove, yet none could simply be ignored. The file shows the accounting still reaching back, in 1983, to single deaths from the war's hardest years in the south.

The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where such testimony carried special weight.
